analysis.one_liner: Bans federally insured banks from making or financing high-cost payday loans and applies rate-disclosure rules to all of them.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote; it sat in a Financial Services subcommittee for the rest of the 107th Congress and died in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit banks insured by the federal government from making payday loans directly or financing them for other lenders, and would bar any payday loan built on a borrower's check or account at an insured bank or credit union. It would also state explicitly that payday loans are covered credit under the Truth in Lending Act, so lenders must disclose the true annual interest rate, and it would raise the penalties for violations. The bill's own findings describe payday loans averaging 474 percent annual interest and typically renewed ten or more times. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in March 2001 and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income borrowers who use payday loans when they are short on cash. The bill targets the arrangement where payday lenders partner with federally insured banks to invoke federal law and evade state interest-rate caps, and it would force lenders to disclose the real annual percentage rate instead of quoting only a fee.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits insured depository institutions from making payday loans, directly or indirectly, and from lending to other lenders to finance, refinance, or extend payday loans.
Cuts off the loophole the bill's findings describe, where payday lenders affiliate with insured banks to use federal preemption and circumvent state usury limits and small-loan rate caps.

Bars any creditor from making a payday loan secured by a personal check drawn on, or an automatic debit to, an account at an insured bank or credit union, closing the main practical channel for these loans.

Amends the Truth in Lending Act to state that payday loans have always been covered credit, requiring standard interest-rate disclosures, and raises civil penalties for violations from $100 to $200 per violation and lifts the class-action cap from $500,000 to a higher formula based on 2 percent of the creditor's net worth.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lending companies and any banks earning fees by financing or warehousing payday loans for them. The bill also removes one form of short-term credit available to borrowers who lack other options, without creating a replacement.

drawbacks.text: The bill would cut off a source of fast cash for people the bill itself describes as having limited access to affordable credit and in desperate need to meet immediate obligations, without creating a cheaper alternative.

It does not cap payday loan interest rates nationwide; outside the banking system, the bill's main levers are disclosure requirements and the ban on loans backed by checks or accounts at insured institutions, so high-cost storefront lending could continue where state law allows.

Raising liability per violation from $100 to $200 and expanding class-action exposure increases litigation and compliance costs for lenders, some of which would likely be passed to borrowers in the form of higher fees where lending remains legal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and specific: it ends the bank-affiliation scheme that let payday lenders evade state interest-rate caps, and it forces honest annual-rate disclosure on a product whose typical two-week loan carried a 474 percent annual rate and was commonly renewed ten or more times. The access objection is genuine but weaker than it sounds, because a loan that rolls over ten times at rates above 1,000 percent annually is a debt treadmill, not liquidity; the honest gap is that the bill restricts supply without building a cheaper alternative.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, then to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit Subcommittee eleven days later, and no committee or subcommittee ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative John LaFalce introduced the bill on March 15, 2001, with nine original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
On March 26, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where the record ends.
The bill received no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action during the remainder of the 107th Congress, which ended January 3, 2003.

The bill's findings cite consumer group studies that the average payday loan carries a 474 percent annual percentage rate for a two-week loan, is typically renewed ten or more times, and that lenders partner with insured banks to circumvent state interest-rate regulation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders and the insured banks that financed or hosted their loans kept operating under the existing structure, and borrowers continued paying triple-digit annual rates with no federal disclosure or enforcement changes. Members of the committee never had to take a recorded position on the bill.

for.name: John J. LaFalce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 16 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Kanjorski, Maloney, Gutierrez, Lee, Jones, Capuano, Clay, Hinchey, and Schakowsky.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, Republican-controlled in the 107th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 15, 2001, sent it to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit Subcommittee on March 26, and never reported the bill out.

against.name: Payday lending industry
against.what_they_did: Fought federal restrictions on payday lending and defended the bank-partnership structure the bill targeted.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were Democrats; the Republican-controlled committee never brought the bill up, and no roll-call was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill bars loans backed by checks or accounts at insured banks or credit unions and applies truth-in-lending disclosure and liability rules to payday loans, directly attacking a product that averaged 474 percent annual interest and rolled over ten or more times. Payday lenders' revenue depends on exactly these fees and rollovers.

Insured depository institutions would be prohibited from making payday loans or financing them for other lenders, ending the fee income from partnerships where payday lenders used the bank's federal preemption to evade state rate caps. A small share of bank fee income, but the structure was central to the industry's growth.

The bill does not ban credit unions from making small-dollar loans (the prohibition covers insured depository institutions), and credit unions could gain members seeking alternatives. But the ban on payday loans backed by checks drawn on insured credit unions restricts their members' access to storefront payday credit.
